Senses.Explanation: No arising is the claim that things do not come into birth or arise. Chan records make it something to embody, awaken to, realize, and question, but they also refuse to identify it with dormant stillness or a secure place in which to settle. Yongjue Yuanxian gives the sharpest direct boundary. He rejects calling ‘the mechanism quiescent and not yet issuing forth’ no arising (指機寂未發謂之無生), then says that things do not arise from themselves, from another, jointly, or without a cause; when none of these four modes arises, there truly is no arising (諸法不自生，不他生，不共生，不無因生，四俱不生，則實無生). In the Yongjia encounter, Huineng asks why Yongjia Xuanjue does not embody no arising and comprehend what has no speed; Yongjia answers that embodiment itself is no arising and comprehension originally has no speed (何以體取無生，了無速乎；體即無生，了本無速). The Visvabhu Buddha section of the Compendium of the Five Lamps attributes a verse saying that mind is originally without arising but exists because of objects (心本無生因境有). Guxue Zhe asks for ‘a phrase of no arising’ (如何是無生底句), Foyin Zhiqing says one can realize it immediately and then asks the assembly whether they want to see it, Puan Yinsu says that once it is awakened to it is never mistaken, and Konggu Daocheng asks for its meaning before comparing it to vast empty space. Chushi Fanqi supplies the strongest recorded reversal: when the mind dwells in no arising, no arising itself is birth and death; he raises the staff and says, ‘this is not no arising’ (心住，無生即生死；拈拄杖，云：這箇不是無生). Longer phrases preserve the base wording but add their own lexical work. Yang Jie criticizes further talk of no arising (更說無生話); Huineng pairs no arising with no extinguishing (無生無滅); Liangshan Yuanguan banishes recognition into ‘the country of no arising’ and then calls that resting place dead water that holds no dragon; Chushi cites ‘endurance concerning no arising beneath the staff’ (棒下無生忍); and Guifeng Zongmi explicitly names the longer phrase ‘endurance concerning no arising’ (無生法忍). These families show how Chan loads and tests the words without turning every compound into evidence for a second bare-headword sense.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 4,980 occurrences in 383 texts. Counted families include ‘originally without arising’ (本無生), 326; ‘endurance concerning no arising’ (無生法忍), 217; ‘no arising and no extinguishing’ (無生無滅), 92; ‘talk of no arising’ (無生話), 166; ‘song of no arising’ (無生曲), 177; and ‘country of no arising’ (無生國), 143. Family rows are explicitly marked and do not buy bare-headword depth. The inherited target ‘unborn’ remains an alternate and search alias, but ‘no arising’ is primary because the corpus's direct definition concerns denied modes of arising rather than gestational status. Predicate, abstract-noun, and question uses concern the same claim and do not warrant grammar-only senses. Personal names containing the graphs are excluded as names, not converted into a lexical sense; named Chan figures belong on the local roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖曰：何以體取無生，了無速乎？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Imperial Selection of Recorded Sayings (御選語錄), in its record of Yongjia Xuanjue's encounter with Huineng, records Huineng asking why Yongjia does not embody no arising and comprehend what has no speed. This row contains Huineng's exact turn only.

The Imperial Selection of Recorded Sayings (御選語錄), in its named Yongjia Xuanjue record, gives Yongjia's reply that embodiment itself is no arising and comprehension originally has no speed. This row is split from Huineng's preceding question so each speaker owns one exact turn.

The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe (古雪哲禪師語錄), in Guxue Zhe's own hall address, records Guxue asking the assembly for a phrase of no arising. Guxue Zhe is source-attested but not yet on the local roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 討甚閒工夫，更說無生話。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)), in the named layman Yang Jie section, records Yang Jie's own verse asking why one should spend idle effort speaking further talk of no arising. This family row anchors ‘talk of no arising’ (無生話) and does not buy bare-headword depth.

Occurrences.Kwic: 假借四大以為身。心本無生因境有。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), in its explicitly headed Visvabhu Buddha section, attributes this verse to Visvabhu Buddha: the mind is originally without arising and exists because of objects. The section figure, not the later compiler, is the verse's named actor. Visvabhu Buddha is source-attested but not yet on the local roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有能恁麼搆去，便謂立證無生，不待僧祗而成正覺。如今要見無生麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Ancestral Outlines (列祖提綱錄) explicitly heads this address ‘Chan Master Foyin Qing’; the parallel passage in the Continued Transmission of the Lamp identifies him fully as Zhihai Foyin Zhiqing. Foyin Zhiqing is the exact speaker who says that this is immediate realization of no arising and asks whether the assembly wants to see it. He is source-attested but not yet on the local roster.

The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dachuan Puji (大川普濟禪師語錄) records Dachuan raising Liangshan Yuanguan's case. In the original exchange Liangshan answers Zhen the garden head by banishing recognition into the country of no arising. Liangshan is the exact quoted speaker; Dachuan is the later raiser. This family row anchors ‘country of no arising’ (無生國) and does not buy bare-headword depth.

The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dachuan Puji (大川普濟禪師語錄), in the same raised Liangshan case, records Liangshan Yuanguan rejecting the proposed resting place with ‘dead water holds no dragon.’ This no-headword contrast anchors the family claim without counting toward bare-headword depth.
